newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: UK's George warns against seeing EMU as panacea.
newsitem.headline: UK's George warns against seeing EMU as panacea.

text.p: Bank of England governor Eddie George said on Wednesday that some potential members of a planned European Union single currency should think twice before opting to take part from the start.
He said that it could lead to greater social tensions for some countries if their economies were not up to the discipline that the single currency implied.
"I am not sure that the criteria in themselves are enough," he said, referring to a series of economic tests that candidate countries must pass next year.
"I think that some (countries) should have a long think," he told journalists on a visit to Lisbon.

George, who was to attend a closed-door Bank of Portugal seminar on Thursday, said that membership of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) should not be presented as a matter of life or death for a country.

He said that the single currency implied a single level of interest rates and this might not be convenient for all countries, particularly those where there was a high level of structural unemployment.
"The most important issue confronting Europe is structural unemployment," he said, adding that some countries should consider their options very carefully before taking any decisions on membership.

George said that the sharp narrowing of interest rate differentials between Germany and high yielders such as Spain and Portugal showed that investors were betting on the political will of the European Union to make EMU happen with a wide membership.
"I hope they are right...but I don't make that sort of bet," George said, adding that he hoped that investors were right because if they were wrong, the result could be tensions in financial markets.
He also said that Britain opposed any attempt to define a stability pact between future participants of a single currency in too rigid a fashion.
"We are pragmatic. We think it is not very wise to introduce hard and fast rules," he said.

Some countries, notably Germany, have been pressing for clear limits to single currency members' freedom to run budget deficits above a certain level. They want fines imposed when the limits are exceeded.
He said that all potential members of EMU agreed on the principles that lay behind the stability pact -- the need for firm fiscal discipline -- but differed on how the pact should operate.
He said that Britain should be in a position to meet the economic tests for membership. Britain "had a perfectly respectable chance of meeting the criteria without any fudge," he added.
